It was in the inner room of Kondō's dōjō, at the top of the slope at Yanagichō in Kohinata, that Itō Kashitarō came face to face with the Shinsengumi's commander Kondō Isami.
"Itō-sensei,"
Kondō called him, so. Ordinarily Kondō's eyes were sharp enough to pierce a man.

But at this sitting he kept up a laughing voice from first to last. The men attending at his side — Takeda Kanryūsai, Ogata Shuntarō, Nagakura Shinpachi — had never seen Kondō in such good humor as this day.
"Ogata-kun, the sensei's cup,"
he would prompt, and the like.
"No, no — quite enough,"
Itō bowed politely.
"Don't hold back. You're said to have a fine head for it. Drink your fill. Today let us talk with nothing held in our bellies, either of us."
"That is just what I wish."

Itō Kashitarō that day was in a haori of the nanako weave then in fashion, a black habutae kimono with his crest and its lining, and Sendai-hira hakama in a narrow vertical stripe; the hilts of his two swords were capped with silver, the guards openwork-carved in a bamboo-and-sparrow design with gold inlay — the whole a magnificent turnout that put one in mind of a great hatamoto. He was a fine-looking man to begin with.
"Ah, a pleasure,"
and Kondō, no drinker, though unused to it emptied three cups and went bright red.
He must have been very glad.
(What manner of man is this?)
Itō, cup after cup, did not slacken his watching. For a man who meant one day to take the Shinsengumi from within, his life hung on this watching. The first impression he got was:
(As they say, no ordinary man after all.)

Not in the sense of a great man. There was in Kondō something abnormal, something that put one in mind of an animal. The very stuff of maleness, one might call it. A wild beast's vigor, and a force of spirit that made a man shudder to be fixed by it, Kondō had brimming in every corner of his frame.
Itō thought of a blade. And no thin blade either, no razor or dagger. Call it a cold-chisel. Strike it with a hammer, and it looked fit to split an iron ingot.
(A man to be feared.)
He thought so, and despised him in the same breath.
(A man only an age of chaos has any use for.)
To beat off Kondō's oppression, Itō strained to despise him.
And then,
(There is an unlooked-for weak point.)
It was that this man, at bottom no more than a cold-chisel, was pitiably fond of politics.
That day Kondō, unlike his usual self, blew a great country-bumpkin's brag.
By this man's account, the reason for his coming down east this time was to talk the shogun round.
"The shogun?"
"Just so."
He would persuade the shogun — Iemochi — to go up to Kyoto and, under the imperial command, take personal command at the head of the Chōshū expedition, or so he said.
"Ho-ho."
Itō, at the outset, was half in doubt.
However the shogunate's power might have decayed, how could a mere rōnin captain gain audience with the shogun?
"You astonish me. That Kondō-sensei was granted audience with the shogun—"
"No,"
Kondō was flustered.

"Not with His Highness the shogun. I called, without exception, upon the rōjū, His Lordship Matsumae Izu-no-kami, and all the other council elders, and set out how gravely the situation in Kyoto presses, and how the shogun's going up is now a matter of the most burning urgency."
"I see."

Even that, surely, was no small thing. To offer the shogunate council political advice was the business of the collateral houses and the fudai daimyō. In the day of the Tairō Ii, several daimyō had suffered punishment for no more than a tozama lord's putting his oar into shogunal policy. And here Kondō, a rōnin, had worked upon the shogunate council. (Though Kondō, to be sure, had had the Aizu domain do him special groundwork beforehand toward meeting the elders.)
(And yet — the shogunate's prestige, too, has come down in the world.)
So Itō could not help thinking.
"And what was the council's mind?"
"Itō-sensei,"
Kondō dropped his voice.
"You will keep this close, will you not?"
"You need not press the point."
Itō nodded with his handsome face.

"Then I disclose it to you as a comrade. Take it for a shogunate secret of the deepest sort. Should it leak to Chōshū, needless to say, or to Satsuma, Inshū, Chikuzen, Tosa — the western lords who would, given the chance, take the mastery of the realm from the Tokugawa — it would come to great trouble."
A secret of such weight, Kondō had had opened to him by the shogunate's own elders. Whether Kondō meant by this to parade himself before Itō Kashitarō, who can say.
"Itō-kun,"
the address had shifted, to the comradely form.
"In the shogunate's treasury there is no longer the money for the shogun to go west and chastise Chōshū."
"No money?"
"That's it. …None."
He nodded.
"The shogunate has—?"

"None, no money. Let the shogun go up to Kyoto, and a vast train of attendants is needed. There is no longer the allowance to pay them. And not the allowance only. Guns are needed. Horses are needed. Provisions and baggage must be got ready. Gunpowder is needed. Ships to carry it all are needed. Itō-kun, that money — there is none."
Kondō put on a look of anguish, for all the world as if he were an elder himself.

By the by, about this time the shogunate was, in the deepest secrecy, negotiating a loan with France for the costs of the Chōshū expedition and of Westernizing the shogunal forces (it came, after twists and turns, to nothing). So hard-pressed was the shogunate.
"But,"
Itō said, with a grave air,

"in Edo there are the hatamoto and gokenin whom the house of Tokugawa has nourished three hundred years. When the shogun goes west raising the war-standard of Tōshō-gongen — of Ieyasu — surely those direct retainers will sell their household goods to buy horses, get their guns together, provide even their road-allowances themselves, and throw down their lives to repay three hundred years' favor?"
"Ah, but there it is,"
Kondō said, with a displeased air.
"Itō-kun too must have heard the talk. The greater part of the hatamoto, pleading the poverty of their households, have no wish to take the field."

Itō too had heard it. Not all the shogunal retainers, of course, but the greater part of them were against a Chōshū expedition led by the shogun in person. There were even those among them who said openly, within Edo castle,
—Where is the need for the shogun to go out in person to chastise a single westland daimyō of a bare three hundred and sixty thousand koku?
and so held forth.

The point was that if the shogun went out, the hatamoto and gokenin must follow him as his men-at-arms. Not the blow to their finances only: to throw over the soft life of Edo and lay their bodies bare in the field of war was a piece of boorishness unthinkable to men who had been called direct retainers, lords, for three hundred years.
"They speak of the eighty thousand mounted hatamoto,"
said Kondō.

"They are so many straw dolls. Itō-kun, the shogun means, by the imperial command, to guard the palace, to put down Chōshū, and beyond that to guard the nation from the foreign barbarian. And who is to guard that shogun? The hatamoto shrink from war. In the end there is none to guard the shogun and guard the imperial city but the Shinsengumi."
Kondō drained his cup at a draught and offered it to Itō.
Itō received it. From the side Ogata Shuntarō filled it with wine.
"Itō-kun, let us swear a covenant."
"By all means."
Itō drained it quietly. What was in his heart, there is no telling.
The day after he met Kondō, Itō gathered his chief pupils and comrades at the dōjō in Sagachō, Fukagawa.
Seven men.
Not one of them a shogunate loyalist.
They were men who meant, given the chance, to plant a flag in Kyoto, set the Son of Heaven at their head, and make good the work of revering the Emperor and expelling the barbarian.

First, Itō's own younger brother Suzuki Mikisaburō (who later took shelter with the Satsuma domain and fired on Kondō; after the Restoration a junior inspector of the Danjō office; died in the eighth year of Taishō, aged eighty-three).
Among Itō's old comrades:
Shinohara Tainoshin (the same; died in the forty-fourth year of Meiji, aged eighty-four).
Kanō Michinosuke (Washio; later cast his lot with the Satsuma domain).
Hattori Takeo (died fighting, before the Restoration).
Sano Shimenosuke (seppuku, before the Restoration).
Of Itō's pupils:
Nakanishi Noboru (later cast his lot with the Satsuma domain).
Utsumi Jirō (the same).

Even among these, the ones called masters of the sword were Hattori Takeo, a man of Bushū, and Shinohara Tainoshin, who had quit the Kurume domain; and Kanō and Sano too were no whit below the present officers of the Shinsengumi.
To these seven Itō recounted his talk with Kondō in full, and further laid open the very bottom of his heart.
—It is a joining, and no more, for now. In time we take the lead of it. By that I would make of the corps a righteous army for toppling the shogunate. What are your minds?
"From the first,"
said Itō.
"We enter the tiger's den. And more than to seize the cub: we drive out the fierce tiger and take the den itself. I would have you put your lives in my hands."
All gave their assent.
But one man only, Shinohara Tainoshin, eldest of the company, felt something perilous in Itō's over-clever stratagem, and,
"Is it safe, do you think?"

he said, in an engaging Kurume drawl. Shinohara was a "fierce loyalist" who, some years before, had gone with Kanō, Hattori, and Sano here present to try to burn down the foreign legations at Yokohama; but he had ordinarily the air of the easy master of a village headman's house. Besides the sword, he could do jūjutsu.
"'Is it safe,' you say — what do you mean by that?"
"Why, I'm a poor hand at play-acting. Let me get into the Shinsengumi with a false heart, and I'm not the man to keep up the sham three days."
"That will do very well."
Itō was trusting to his own cleverness.
"The acting I do myself. All you gentlemen need do is keep to your duties in silence, just as Kondō and Hijikata command. And when the moment comes — rise."
"That's easy enough,"
Shinohara said, laughing,
"but the troupe leader, now—"
"You mean me?"
"Just so. It's an ungracious thing to say, but a man too clever may tumble off the runway for the very cleverness of it — and that would never do."
"Shinohara-kun—"
"No, hear me out. The Shinsengumi is not made up of nothing but fools and clay dolls. There's a shrewd hand at judging a play among them. From what I hear — Hijikata Toshizō."
"No — I've already looked into him. Hijikata is an unlettered man. Not worth the reckoning."
"I wonder about that."
"Shinohara-kun, this is unlike you — you seem to have taken fright."
"Not a bit of it."
Shinohara laughed.
"Once a thing's settled as this is, I've handed my life and my scheming over to the clever head of you. It's only that, at the swearing, I'd say my one word of misgiving and no more."
"Misgiving. By Tōdō-kun's account the Shinsengumi is a mere rabble. You fear it too much, Shinohara-kun."
"It's not the Kondō or the Hijikata of the Shinsengumi that I fear."
"What, then?"

"Your cleverness. Or rather, your leaning on it too far. Look round this company, and it's all ham actors, with the one thousand-ryō star among us yourself alone. Being too skilled a hand — take care you don't float up clear of the rest."
"Shinohara-kun—"
"There, the talk is done. The rest I've left in your hands, my life with it. —Wine, Hattori-kun."
"What is it?"
"Let us all buy wine. For a last drink of Edo's wine, tonight I drink till I drop."

That night, after all had gone, Itō wrote to his old mother Koyo, who lived alone in his home village of Sanmura in Hitachi, telling her he was going up to Kyoto; told his wife Ume the whole course of the covenant and the journey; and a few days after, closed the dōjō in Sagachō, Fukagawa, and moved his family to a rented house in Mitadaimachi.
As said before, Itō, who had been Daizō, changed his name to Kashitarō on quitting Edo. In his own way, he must have steeled himself to no small resolve.

That Itō went up to Kyoto with a resolve fully steeled there is another anecdote to show. His wife Ume seems, by the writing of her letters and the rest, to have been a woman of considerable cultivation; but she too, no doubt, fretted overmuch for her husband's safety in Kyoto. She sent a false report — that Itō's mother was gravely ill — and to Itō, who came hurrying back to Edo by express palanquin in his alarm,

—In truth, your mother's illness is a lie. Because your position weighs on me so, I wrote hoping you would give up rushing about on the nation's affairs (this passage word for word from Ono Keijirō's "My Uncle, Itō Kashitarō").
What Itō felt toward Ume at this time is not well known. Only that, "in a great rage,"
—A creature like you knows nothing but herself, and nothing of the weight of the nation.

he divorced her, and had done. Among the first-rank loyalists of the Restoration years there were a surprising number of devoted husbands, but Itō Kashitarō was likely the only one who divorced his wife on the nation's account (by the by, his old mother Koyo was the kind of woman who hung a portrait of Kashitarō in the alcove and prayed morning and evening for his health. She died in the twenty-fifth year of Meiji at the house of her second son Mikisaburō in Ishioka-machi, Hitachi, aged eighty-two. Her death-poem: A keepsake, this, of the reign that never ends through all the ten thousand ages).
Itō Kashitarō and his party of eight entered Kyoto on the first day of the twelfth month of the first year of Genji.
That day it was bitterly cold.
Toshizō was eating his midday meal alone in his room. A vice-commander was assigned a single page, half a trooper-in-training, but Toshizō would not be waited on at all.
He drew the rice-tub to his side and, dishing it into his bowl himself, ate alone. From boyhood he had been a man who disliked eating in company. In this too he was like a cat.
"Who's there?"
he said, staying his chopsticks.
A shadow moved on the paper door.
It slid open without ceremony, and Okita Sōji came in.
"Oh — it's you, Sōji."
This youth alone he found hard to handle.
"Please, go on eating."
"Something urgent?"

"No, I'll watch from here. I don't know if it's because I eat so little myself, but I dearly love to watch another man eat with a will. Watching you eat, Hijikata-san, in particular, I feel the strength welling up in me."
"You're a disagreeable fellow."
He drank his tea.
"Is it business?"
"You've heard, then?"
"Heard what?"
"There are eight guests come from Edo at Kondō-sensei's rest-lodging — the villa of the Kōshō-ji monzeki."
"Hm."
He set down his teacup.
"Itō, is it."
"Sharp as ever. This Itō is a pale, good-looking man, like an actor; but the rest are a set of ogreish champions — Benkei, Ise Yoshimori, and their like."
"Are they, now."
He began to use his toothpick.
"Yamanami-sensei and Tōdō-san, being of the same school, went off at once to pay their respects, it seems."
"Odd. No word of the party's arrival has come to me, the vice-commander."
"I forgot to say. I am that messenger. Kondō-sensei charged me to summon you, Hijikata-san."
"Fool — why not say so sooner?"
"But,"
Okita chuckled.
"And what's funny?"
"It's such a treat — the way your face changes, Hijikata-san."
"What are you talking about."
"Will you go to the Kōshō-ji villa at once?"
"I won't."
He was picking with the toothpick. Toshizō had a reason of his own. Why should the vice-commander of the Shinsengumi go out to the lodging of a newly-joined trooper?
"If he wants to see my face, the thing is to have this Itō-san take the trouble to come to the vice-commander's room at the barracks."
He threw the toothpick down.
Okita snorted a laugh. Tease as he might, it was a Toshizō like this that he loved.
